# Steamship and screw propeller (`steamship_screw_propeller`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/navigation.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Navigation, transport & exploration (`navigation`)
- Deps: helped by rotative_steam_engine, high_pressure_steam, separate_condenser, watertight_bulkheads
- Core idea: A steam engine turning paddle wheels or a screw frees ships from the wind and lets them run on schedule upstream and against headwinds. The screw (a twisted blade turning under the stern) is more efficient than paddles at sea, is not lifted out of the water as the ship rolls, and leaves the sides free for guns. The limit is coal: early engines burned several kilograms per horsepower-hour, so ocean steamers carried sail and needed coaling stations until compound and triple-expansion engines (1860s–1880s) made long routes pay.
- Pitfalls:
  - Ignoring the trade-off between coal and paying cargo; the wooden Great Western made scheduled Atlantic passages
  - Ignoring boiler explosions and fires, the main killers of early steamboats
  - Saying Fulton invented the steamboat; several had run before his North River Steamboat (1807)
- History: europe: 1783 – Jouffroy d'Abbans' Pyroscaphe on the Saône; 1803 Symington's Charlotte Dundas; 1836 screw patents by Francis Pettit Smith and John Ericsson; 1838 Sirius and Great Western cross the Atlantic under steam; 1843 Brunel's iron screw ship Great Britain; 1845 Rattler beats the paddle Alecto in a tug of war; americas: 1787 – John Fitch on the Delaware; 1807 Fulton's North River Steamboat on the Hudson
- Read:
  - Stephen Fox, Transatlantic: Samuel Cunard, Isambard Brunel, and the Great Atlantic Steamships (2003)
  - L. T. C. Rolt, Isambard Kingdom Brunel (1957)
